tier_reason: Every quoted number appears in the README Performance Comparison table and matches the per-library result JSONs in the first-party benchmark repo (albumentations-team/benchmark at commit ab6e84d: benchmark/runner.py, benchmark/utils.py, benchmark/transforms/*_impl.py, output/*_results.json). The code and library versions are public, but the CPU is given only as 'arm', 16 cores, on macOS 15.1 with no chip model, and the runs were done by the project itself, so the tier is C, not A.

corrections.workload: Images per second on one CPU thread for each transform (Resize to 512, RandomResizedCrop 512, Hue, Saturation, Grayscale, Brightness, Contrast, ColorJitter and others), 2000 ImageNet-style images, adaptive warm-up, then 5 timed passes (median reported). Albumentations and imgaug get uint8 NumPy arrays read with OpenCV, torchvision gets uint8 tensors, Kornia gets float32 [0,1] tensors and AugLy gets PIL images.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Python wheels, no compiler flags. Competitor runs: Python 3.12.8 (Anaconda), torch 2.5.1, kornia 0.8.0, torchvision 0.20.1, imgaug 0.4.0 (opencv-python 4.11.0.86, numpy 1.26.4), augly 1.0.0 (pillow 11.1.0), run 2025-01-23 to 2025-01-25. Albumentations run: Python 3.12.7 (Anaconda), albumentations 2.0.4, opencv-python-headless 4.11.0.86, numpy 2.2.3, run 2025-02-18.
corrections.hardware: macOS 15.1 arm64 (Apple silicon; exact chip not stated), 16 CPU cores. Single thread enforced through OMP/OpenBLAS/MKL/vecLib/NumExpr=1 and OpenCV threads=1. The Albumentations and competitor results come from separate sessions about four weeks apart.
corrections.caveats: This is an augmentation library, not a general resampler or color-management library. It is compared against other augmentation libraries rather than the category baselines (ImageMagick, stb_image_resize). Its speed comes from OpenCV kernels: against imgaug, which also calls cv2 INTER_LINEAR, Resize is only 1.18x faster. Several rows compare different work. torchvision v2.Resize(512) resizes the shorter side to 512 with antialias=True, while Albumentations produces 512x512 with INTER_LINEAR and no antialiasing. Kornia receives float32 tensors although the README says uint8, so the 12.98x Hue and the Saturation/ColorJitter ratios against Kornia pit uint8 OpenCV LUT code against float32 tensor math. Kornia's RandomGrayscale returns 3 channels where Albumentations returns 1. AugLy's ColorJitter is called without a hue term, so it does less work than Albumentations. The Albumentations run and the competitor runs used different Python builds on different dates. The README table does not link the benchmark repo, which has since been rewritten for AlbumentationsX; the matching code and results are at commit ab6e84d. The repo was archived on 2025-07-10; its successor AlbumentationsX is AGPL-3.0 or commercial, and only this archived MIT version is copyable. The peer-reviewed paper (MDPI Information 11(2):125, 2020) also has benchmarks, but mdpi.com is egress-blocked, so it was not checked.

notes: Kept despite being off the category baselines (Python augmentation library against other augmentation libraries), as the batch notes asked. The numbers are genuine harness output from public code, not fabricated. Equivalence of work differs per transform (output size and antialiasing for Resize, float32 input for Kornia, channel count for Grayscale), and the caveats now list each case.

tier_reason: The README shows the ns/iter output of the crate's own libtest #[bench] functions (src/lib.rs, tests::bench). Those benchmarks compare the crate only against a naive powf reference written in the same file, and no rustc version, flags or CPU is given. That makes the evidence first-party with partial methodology, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README bench output, one iteration = 51 conversions (204 for the x4 pair, 256 for sRGB8 to f32): f32 to sRGB8 scalar 144 ns/iter vs 971 ns for the naive powf reference (about 6.7x, derived from page data); f32x4 SSE2 440 ns vs 3,625 ns for four naive calls (about 8.2x, derived from page data), but only about 1.1x over four scalar fast calls (482 ns, derived from page data); sRGB8 to f32 lookup table 81 ns vs 4,026 ns (about 50x, derived from page data). The README prose says '~5x' and '~20x'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly libtest #[bench] (needs --cfg unstable_bench); rustc version, optimization flags and target CPU not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 23 stars; crates.io 18.3M downloads (10.5M recent) as of 2026-10-04
corrections.caveats: The baseline is a naive per-call powf reference written inside the crate's own bench module, not an incumbent library. f32_to_srgb8 is ryg's public-domain table-plus-lerp routine, and its 104-entry table is byte-identical to fp32_to_srgb8_tab4 in stb_image_resize2.h (stbir__linear_to_srgb_uchar), so the category incumbent already uses this exact technique and the crate gives no speedup over stb's own sRGB path. The output is not bitwise equal to the rounded powf reference for every input: the max error is 0.544 against the exact value (the D3D bound is 0.6), and the exhaustive test checks that error bound, monotonicity, SIMD equal to scalar, and round-tripping, not equality with the rounded reference. srgb8_to_f32 matches the powf reference exactly for all 256 inputs. The README prose ratios (~5x, ~20x) are smaller than the ratios the bench numbers imply. No CPU, compiler or flags are stated. Last commit 2021-05-09. Not compared against ImageMagick, lcms or stb. If the CC0-1.0 option is chosen there is no patent grant; Apache-2.0 and MIT are also offered.

notes: Kept at C. The baseline sits inside the same repo and is not an incumbent. The lookup is approximate (within 0.6 ULP), not exact to the rounded reference. stb_image_resize2.h contains the same ryg table (checked byte for byte), so this is a separate Rust port of a routine the stb incumbent already ships, not a port of stb itself. The orchestrator may prefer a duplicate or reference note against nothings/stb.

tier_reason: The numbers appear verbatim in the README Performance section mirrored in the PyPI description of tinyscaler 1.2.8, with the CPU stated (AMD 1950x). The benchmark script (examples/benchmark.py) cannot be reached, because the GitHub repo returns 404 and the script is not in the sdist, and no compiler or flags are stated. First-party README text only, so tier C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: C kernels (SSE3 via pmmintrin.h on x86_64, Neon on Arm) built as a Cython extension; setup.py adds no optimization flags on x86_64/arm64 (-mfpu=neon only on 32-bit Arm), so Python's default extension flags apply; compiler, flags and library versions for the benchmark run not stated
corrections.caveats: The GitHub repo page and raw.githubusercontent.com (README, examples/benchmark.py) all returned 404 on 2026-10-04, and no mirror or fork was found. A WebSearch snippet of the old repo page says the project was deprecated on 2025-08-11 for lack of community use (snippet only). The README text was read from the PyPI description of tinyscaler 1.2.8 (uploaded 2024-08-02), and the C source and MIT license come from its sdist. The benchmark script is not in the sdist, so the run could not be inspected, and it is unknown which dtype and channel layout the other libraries received. TinyScaler itself converts uint8/RGB input to float32 RGBA. The bilinear kernel (src/scaler.c scale_bilinear_4f32) is a 2x2-tap point-sampled bilinear without antialiasing, while Pillow's BILINEAR downscale widens its filter support with the scale factor. The 15.9x win over Pillow therefore compares different work and output quality. OpenCV INTER_LINEAR is the like-for-like comparison and is 1.6x faster than TinyScaler. The area kernel (scale_area_4f32) is an approximate box filter: its loop never reaches src_upper, so the upper partial row/column gets full weight and the lower edge weights are approximate. It does not do exact fractional-area integration like OpenCV INTER_AREA, so the 1.9x area win is also not equal work. Compiler flags and library versions are not stated. Not compared against ImageMagick or stb_image_resize.

notes: The repo is 404 on github.com (page and raw), as the batch notes said. Tiered C on the PyPI-mirrored README, and the source was checked from the 1.2.8 sdist on files.pythonhosted.org. Both quoted wins compare unequal work (no antialiasing against Pillow, approximate area weights against OpenCV INTER_AREA); the like-for-like bilinear comparison shows OpenCV faster.
